summary: Defines a SIP event package that lets a user subscribe to another user and receive notifications when the state of that user's INVITE-initiated dialogs changes. It also defines the data format used in the notifications. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4235 lets one Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) user subscribe to changes in another user's calls. Notifications describe whether each reported dialog is trying, ringing, connected, or terminated, subject to authorization.

questions: how to watch call state in sip
what is the sip dialog event package
subtitle: Subscribe to changes in a user's SIP call dialogs and receive structured notifications.

tldr.problem: Applications may need to know whether a user's calls are starting, active, or finished, even when the application is not on the user's device.
tldr.mechanism: A subscriber sends a SUBSCRIBE for the dialog event package. The notifier sends NOTIFY messages with an XML document describing dialog states and changes.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the dialog event package, its XML format, and two feature parameters. RFC 4235 was later updated by RFC 7463 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4235 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 7463 and RFC 8996. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Applications Need Call State
sections.content:
The SIP Events framework lets a client subscribe to a defined set of events and receive notifications. RFC 4235 defines the dialog package for INVITE-initiated dialogs, the relationships between SIP peers created by calls.

Applications such as automatic callback or conferencing can use these notifications without sitting in the call path. The RFC also defines two feature parameters that describe user-agent capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: A separate application can ask a phone to report changes in its calls. This supports features such as notifying someone when a busy user finishes a call.

sections.title: The Dialog Event Package
sections.content:
The package name is dialog and appears in the Event and Allow-Events header fields. A subscription can identify one dialog with call-id, to-tag, and from-tag parameters, or track dialogs created by one INVITE using call-id and to-tag.

Without a filter body, the notifier reports changes to the requested dialogs or to all visible dialogs. Subscribers and notifiers MUST support the application/dialog-info+xml format. Session descriptions are omitted unless requested and authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscriber can ask about a specific call or all calls visible to it. The notifier sends structured XML updates and leaves out session descriptions unless the subscriber is allowed to receive them.

sections.title: States in a Dialog's Life
sections.content:
The RFC defines one finite state machine for callers and callees. It begins in Trying when an INVITE is sent or received, can move to Proceeding or Early after provisional responses, and reaches Confirmed after a successful response.

A forked request can create multiple state-machine instances when responses have different tags. The machine reaches Terminated with an event such as cancelled, rejected, replaced, error, timeout, local-bye, or remote-bye.
sections.plainLanguage: The state machine tracks a call from the initial invitation through provisional responses to an active call or termination. A single invitation can produce several tracked dialogs if it reaches multiple destinations.

sections.title: Sending Updates and Protecting Details
sections.content:
Notifiers may send a NOTIFY when a state transition occurs and SHOULD report changes to dialog characteristics. A notification normally contains only changed dialogs; the response to a subscription contains the full authorized view.

Dialog information is sensitive, so subscriptions SHOULD be authenticated and authorized. The RFC recommends limited information for unauthenticated or third-party subscribers, while an authenticated device for the same address-of-record can receive fuller details.
sections.plainLanguage: A notifier can send a partial update when a call changes and a full view when a subscription begins. It checks who is asking because call details can reveal private information.

sections.title: The XML Dialog Information
sections.content:
The dialog information document is XML 1.0 encoded in UTF-8. Its root element includes a version, a full-or-partial state indicator, and the identity of the observed user. Each dialog has an identifier and a required state element.

A subscriber keeps a table of dialogs. A full document replaces that table; a partial document updates it. If the version jumps ahead and the document is partial, the subscriber SHOULD request a full refresh; a lower version is discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Each XML notification carries a version number and says whether it contains all call information or only changes. The subscriber uses these details to keep a current list and discard stale updates.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The RFC says call state reveals sensitive information and relies on authentication and authorization to control access. It also recommends protecting notifications and feature parameters against alteration.

RFC 4235 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 7463 and RFC 8996. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.
sections.plainLanguage: Call information should be shown only to authorized subscribers, and capability details should be protected from changes. RFC 7463 and RFC 8996 later updated this Proposed Standard.
